## Analysis

### 1. Outside View
The series has been on a steady decline from 455.5 (June 14) to 197.6 (Aug 16), a ~57% drop over 9 weeks. The rate of decline is clearly decelerating: -13.0%, -3.8%, -2.9% over the last three releases. The series is now well below the historical median of 337K, sitting in the lower portion of the distribution. Recent week-over-week changes are much smaller than the historical mean absolute change of 31.7%, suggesting we're in a low-volatility regime. A naive extrapolation of the decelerating decline would predict ~192-195.

### 2. Inside View
The target week is Mon Aug 24 - Sun Aug 30, 2026. From the search results:
- The most notable recent event is the Supreme Court turning down Trump's bid to overturn the $5M E. Jean Carroll verdict (Aug 17, just before the target week) — but this was announced in June, so the news itself isn't fresh.
- Truth Social lawsuit (Aug 12) and midterm election interference report (Aug 12) are now ~2 weeks old.
- No major rallies, indictments, or elections identified specifically for Aug 24-30.
- Midterm elections are approaching (November 2026), which may provide a slight baseline attention uplift.
- August is typically a slower news month.

Net effect: No major spike driver identified. The decelerating decline and lack of major events point to a value slightly below last week's 197.6.

### 3. Pre-mortem
Most likely reason for being wrong: A major event during the target week not captured in my Aug 18 search results — such as a new legal ruling, a campaign rally generating viral attention, or a midterm primary upset involving Trump. Alternatively, the midterm election cycle could start driving more attention as November approaches, causing a reversal of the downward trend.

### 4. Calibration
The historical mean absolute week-over-week change is 31.7%, but recent weeks show 3-13% changes. A SD of ~32 (~16.5% of the base value) balances the recent low-volatility regime against the possibility of unexpected spikes, which the series is clearly capable of.
